h.select_rule: Discard any hypothesis whose condition is the edited field's own current value, or whose condition merely disables or disconnects the edited component. From the rest, keep 10 with distinct mechanisms and field pairs, favouring those where an informed expert could plausibly bet on either direction.
h.strategy: Two patterns are banned because experts find them obvious: (1) conditioning on the current value of the same field being edited, which just restates that upgrading a weak setting helps more than upgrading a strong one; (2) conditions that make the edited component unused, unreachable or inert. Instead, each hypothesis must link two DIFFERENT fields that interact through a non-trivial mechanism, such as substitution between parallel routes, a capacity already supplied elsewhere, one part acting as a bottleneck for another, or interference that turns a usually helpful edit harmful. No condition setting may appear in more than two hypotheses. Use the gaps and negated assumptions as the source of each idea. In each 'why', name the mechanism and explain why the opposite direction is also a priori plausible.

hyps.why: With L2 scaled per minibatch and many steps per epoch at batch 4-10, effective decay is far stronger, so raising alpha over-shrinks weights much more at small batches.
Very wide nets on small tabular datasets have spare capacity that overfits, so stronger L2 is more beneficial there than in narrow, capacity-limited nets.
L2 shrinkage compounds multiplicatively across three ReLU layers and collapses signal propagation, so alpha-up hurts more at depth 3.
Under standard parameterization the stable learning rate shrinks with width, so at LR 0.0774-1 widening pushes training toward divergence or dead ReLUs.
Stacking another 16-40-unit ReLU layer creates a bottleneck that risks dead units and is harder to optimize, so depth-up hurts more when the net is narrow.
Deeper nets need more updates, and batch 161-256 gives few steps in 243 epochs, so the step budget keeps the added layer from paying off.
Step-induced perturbations compound through three layers and lower the stable learning-rate ceiling, so LR-up crosses it sooner in deep nets.
Gradient noise scales roughly with LR/batch, so at batch 4-10 raising the learning rate amplifies already high noise into instability.
At tiny learning rates the update count limits progress, so enlarging the batch cuts steps and leaves the net more underfit within 243 epochs.
With a strong coupled L2 penalty dominating Adam's normalized gradient, larger steps let the data term move the weights before decay pulls them back.
